## Abstract

When recalling autobiographical events, people retrieve not only the event details, but also the

feelings they experienced. Past work with different measures of memories for feelings remain

inconclusive, suggesting that people are either highly consistent or inconsistent with

remembering feelings. The current study examined whether people are able to consistently recall

the intensity of previous feelings associated with consequential and negatively valenced

emotional events, i.e., the 9/11 attack (N = 769) and Covid-19 pandemic (N = 726). By

comparing the initial and recalled intensities of negative feelings, we found that people

systematically recall more intense negative feelings than they initially reported – overestimating

the intensity of past negative emotional experience. The Covid-19 dataset further showed that

people whose emotional well-being improved more demonstrate smaller biases in remembered

feelings. Across both datasets, the remembered intensity of feelings correlated with initial

feelings and were also influenced by current feelings, although the impact of the current feelings

was stronger in the Covid-19 dataset than the 9/11 dataset. Our results suggest that when

recalling negative autobiographical events, people tend to overestimate the intensity of

experienced negative emotional experience with the degree of bias influenced by current feelings

and well-being.

Keywords: Memory, Emotion, Appraisal, Autobiographical memory, Well-being

Overestimating the intensity of negative emotion in autobiographical memory:

evidence from the 9/11 attack and Covid-19 pandemic

Memories for emotional, autobiographical events not only encompass details of what

occurred, but also associated feelings. A common feature of these memories is that even though

they are often vividly recollected, they are sometimes inaccurate or change over time (Talarico &

Rubin, 2003; Rimmele et al., 2011). For example, studies of flashbulb memories -

autobiographical memories for the circumstances of learning about a consequential, surprising

event (Brown & Kulik, 1977) - have shown that many recollected details differ over time

(Neisser & Harsch, 1992). When investigating the consistency of flashbulb memories, past

research typically examined changes in memory for six canonical features: location/place,

ongoing activity, informant, others present, own affect, and aftermath (Brown & Kulik, 1977).

However, different details associated with emotional and consequential events vary in how well

they are remembered (Rimmele et al., 2012). Of all the canonical features related to flashbulb

memories of the 9/11 attack, memory of one’s subjective feelings at the time of the attack i.e.,

own affect, was the least consistent (Hirst et al., 2009).

In the present study, we examine factors that contribute to memories for the intensity of

feelings associated with autobiographical events. Memories for feelings differ from other event

details in many ways. Feelings are internally generated and therefore dissociable from external

perceptual cues. Thus, the event that generated subjective feelings in the past may elicit feelings

upon recollection which may or may not align with past feelings. Unlike external event details,

feelings can vary not only in their basic identity - how they are categorized or labeled (e.g., fear,

happiness) - but also in intensity. Importantly, unlike most external event details, feelings

associated with memories can affect individuals' current psychological health and well-being


<!-- Page 7 -->


OVERESTIMATING NEGATIVE FEELINGS INTENSITY IN MEMORY

6

(Hamann, 2001; Safer et al., 2001). We take advantage of two consequential public events that

occurred in the world, the 9/11 terrorist attack and Covid-19 pandemic, to explore factors that

may contribute to memories for feelings. Specifically, we examine (1) the consistency or

accuracy of the intensity of remembered feelings, (2) how current feelings influence memories

for past feelings , and (3) the relation between remembered feelings and current well-being.

Regarding our first research question, studies investigating the consistency or accuracy of

remembered feelings for autobiographical events have examined personally salient events that

vary in valence and how consequential they are. Both the evaluation of memory consistency and

accuracy involve assessments of the same measure across multiple time points, but the measures

differ with regard to what is remembered. Studies examining memory accuracy (Levine et al.,

2001; Levine et al., 2021) ask participants how they feel currently in relation to a consequential

event, and at a later time ask how they remember feeling at the time they were previously asked.

In the present study, we use data from a survey we conducted during the Covid-19 pandemic to

assess memory accuracy. Studies assessing memory consistency ask participants to report how

they felt during a recently experienced consequential event, and at a later time ask them again to

report how they felt during that same event. Since the initial assessment is already a recollection

of previous feelings, it is not possible to know if the initial report accurately reflected feelings at

the time of the event, it is only possible to determine if the memory is consistent over time. Here,

we use data from a study conducted in the wake of the 9/11 attack to assess memory consistency,

where participants were asked to report how they felt 2 weeks after the attack and 1, 3, and 10

years later.

Using this same 9/11 dataset, Hirst et al. (2009) investigated the consistency of memories

for feelings related to the 9/11 attack. However, their measure of consistency differed from most


<!-- Page 8 -->


OVERESTIMATING NEGATIVE FEELINGS INTENSITY IN MEMORY

7

studies examining memories for feelings. The vast majority of previous studies examining

memories for feelings associated with autobiographical memories compare the intensity of

initial and recalled feelings, examining specific emotional experiences across time. These

measures reflect directional biases: Positive/negative emotions are often associated with biases in

recalling higher/lower felt intensities (Levine et al., 2009; Schmidt et al., 2021). In contrast, Hirst

et al. (2009) examined how participants labeled the nature of their emotional reaction.

Participants completed a free recall paradigm where they reported how they felt during the 9/11

attacks 1-2 weeks, 1 year, 3 years, and 10 years after the 9/11 attack occurred. If participants

provided the same or similar emotion label (e.g., afraid/fear) at each timepoint, their memory

was marked as consistent, whereas if a different emotional label was used (e.g., afraid/sad) their

memory was considered inconsistent. Using this measure, Hirst et al. (2009) found memories for

feelings were highly inconsistent over time; the same or similar emotion label was used to

describe feelings related to the 9/11 attack a week and year later only about forty percent of the

time. In addition, in a follow-up analysis, Hirst et al. (2009) used retrospective ratings of

intensity for feelings - including sadness, anger, fear, confusion, frustration, and shock - to rank-

order the relative strength of remembered emotional reactions and examined how this rank-order

differed over time. Using this rank-order of relative emotional reactions, they once again found

that memories for feelings were highly inconsistent over time.

In contrast to the findings of Hirst et al. (2009) in which the identity or relative intensity

of different emotional reactions was assessed over time, studies examining the consistency or

accuracy of the intensity of specific emotional reactions to a consequential, autobiographical

event have found remembered feelings to be generally accurate. One study examined memory

for the grief associated with the death of a spouse (Safer et al., 2001). To characterize the


<!-- Page 9 -->


OVERESTIMATING NEGATIVE FEELINGS INTENSITY IN MEMORY

8

accuracy of remembered grief, the authors administered a questionnaire probing the current

intensity of grief 6 months after the death of their spouse and evaluated how this initial report

was remembered 4.5 years later. They found no statistically significant difference between the

intensity of initially reported and recalled grief, which was on average only 2.1 percent less

intense than the initial rating (Safer et al., 2001). However, these roughly accurate recollections

of the intensity of past feelings did not preclude remembered feelings from being susceptible to

bias. Associations between recalled grief and current feelings in this study implicate a

retrospective bias with the authors concluding that current feelings are more predictive of

remembered feelings than initial feelings. Since the death of a spouse is a significant personal

event (Frijda, 1992), retrospective biases in recollection may impact current well-being. For

example, overestimating the intensity of a previous negative experience may enable individuals

who have not adapted well to maintain a positive self-image. Consistent with this view, Safer et

al. (2001) observed that widows who experienced relatively little improvement in well-being

over time overestimated prior grief more in their recollections. These findings indicate that

although memory for the intensity of specific remembered feelings is generally accurate,

retrospective biases still influence these memories.

Other studies examining memories for the intensity of feelings experienced during salient

events examined reactions to political events, which may vary in valence and perceived

consequentiality depending on the views of participants (e.g., Levine 1997; Levine et al., 2001,

2020, 2021; Schmidt et al., 2021). In one study, Schmidt and colleagues (2021) investigated two

sources of bias when people recalled  their feelings for past political events: current appraisals

and feelings. To characterize the consistency of feelings and appraisals, the researchers had

participants rate how intensely they felt 12 emotions in the moment they learned the news about


<!-- Page 10 -->


OVERESTIMATING NEGATIVE FEELINGS INTENSITY IN MEMORY

9

the U.K. leaving the E.U., as well as how consequential Brexit was for the U.K. and themselves

– two weeks and 18 months after Brexit. Similar to Safer et al. (2001), on average there was no

statistically significant difference between the intensity of remembered and experienced negative

feelings. However, a closer examination reveals more variability at the individual level, with

46.9% of participants overestimating emotional intensity and 42.7% underestimating it (Schmidt

et al., 2021). Exploring these individual differences revealed that the intensity of remembered

feelings is shaped by current appraisals and current emotion: People who viewed Brexit as more

consequential for the U.K. at the time, and those who currently feel worse, recalled stronger

negative feelings than their initial report.

These findings fit well with another study assessing whether individuals with more

consistent recollections of details about when they heard about a political event are less

susceptible to bias when remembering how the event made them feel (Levine et al., 2021). In

this study, participants reported how intensely happy, angry, and fearful the election outcome

made them feel two days vs. six months following the 2016 US presidential election. When

averaging over happiness, anger, and fearfulness, the authors did not find a statistically

significant difference between overall experienced and remembered emotions However, there

was individual variability: 41% of participants remembered a more intense negative response,

37% remembered a more intense positive response, and 22% remembered the exact rating they

initially reported. With respect to biases in the inaccuracy of remembered feelings, the

magnitude and direction of bias was strongly related to how an individual’s feelings about the

election changed over time: The more negative participants currently felt regarding the election

outcome, the more they overestimated the intensity of previous negative emotions like anger and

fear. However, participants whose feelings were consistent over time, and those who appraised


<!-- Page 11 -->


OVERESTIMATING NEGATIVE FEELINGS INTENSITY IN MEMORY

10

the election outcome as more important, were more likely to remember the intensity of their

feelings accurately. These results support the notion that memory biases may stem from current

emotions and appraisals during recall (Levine, 1997).

Altogether, these findings demonstrate that at a group-level the intensity of remembered

feelings as compared to initial reports of those feelings are comparable, but biases in the

recollection of emotional intensity are apparent at the individual level and differ amongst studies.

In contrast to the death of a loved one, emotional reactions to political events are likely more

varied as they depend on an individual's political views. Therefore, although the death of a loved

one and election outcomes are both personally consequential, feelings associated with election

outcomes are likely to be less uniform across participants. Considering remembered feelings

across these three events in light of this variation suggests that consequential events are not all

remembered similarly, and differences in the accuracy or consistency of memory may depend on

one’s appraisal of the emotional valence and consequentiality of the event.

The conclusion reached by these studies differ from Hirst et al. (2009) in whether people

were consistent in reporting remembered feelings. This discrepancy may be driven by how

remembered feelings were probed. Hirst and colleagues (2009) asked participants to label their

previous feelings by reporting the identity of the emotion they had experienced. In comparison,

being asked to report the remembered intensity of a list of specific emotions provides more

contextual cues. This could potentially make it easier to recollect previous experiences by

limiting response possibilities. Our current study uses the same 9/11 dataset as Hirst et al. (2009)

but examines whether people consistently recall the intensity of previous negative emotions

associated with the 9/11 attack. We further used the Covid-19 dataset to examine the accuracy of

remembered stress. Specifically, we focused on perceived stress participants personally


<!-- Page 12 -->


OVERESTIMATING NEGATIVE FEELINGS INTENSITY IN MEMORY

11

experienced during Covid-19. In contrast to actual stressors, perceived stress is more similar to

negative emotions, both stemming from people’s appraisal of their internal states. In this paper,

we use the term negative feelings to refer to both perceived stress and negative emotions. With

data collected during the Covid-19 pandemic, we examined whether the intensity of remembered

feelings associated with negatively valenced emotional events are susceptible to the same kind of

retrospective biases seen with election outcomes.

To date, research investigating the consistency of remembered feelings for

autobiographical events has emphasized punctate emotional events (Hirst et al., 2009; Safer et

al., 2001; Levine et al., 2021; Schmidt et al., 2021). This differs from the Covid-19 pandemic,

which is an ongoing, prolonged emotional event. By comparing the magnitude of memory biases

across these two datasets, the current study enables us to examine how the nature of the

emotional event and the types of feelings probed relate to the accuracy and consistency of

remembered feelings.

## Methods

9/11 Study

Detailed descriptions of recruitment, data collection, and survey content associated with

the 9/11 study are provided elsewhere (Hirst et al., 2009; 2015). Our current analyses emphasize

people’s emotional experiences.

Participants

The 9/11 study included four surveys administered over 10 years. The first was

administered shortly following the 9/11 terrorist attack (Sept 17 - Sept 21, 2001) across seven

locations: Boston and Cambridge, MA; New Haven, CT; New York, NY; Washington, DC; St.

Louis, MO; Palo Alto, CA; Santa Cruz, CA. Three follow-up surveys were administered


<!-- Page 13 -->


OVERESTIMATING NEGATIVE FEELINGS INTENSITY IN MEMORY

12

approximately 1, 3 and 10 years after 9/11 (Survey 2: Aug 5 - Aug 20, 2002; Survey 3: Aug 9 -

Aug 20, 2004; Survey 4: Aug 1 - Aug 15, 2011). All surveys included questions probing

participants’ memory about the 9/11 attack. Survey 1 was conducted on paper, and surveys 2-4

were conducted on paper or via a website. For analyses, we only included people who completed

survey 1 and at least one follow-up survey, resulting in a total of 880 subjects (614 Female, 261

Male, 5 Unreported; Age M = 38.63, SD = 21.48; Race and Ethnicity: 21 Hispanic (2.4%), 664

White (75.5%), 46 Asian (5.2%), 23 Black (2.6%), 38 More than one race (4.3%), 4 Other

(0.5%), 84 Unreported (9.5%)). Among them, 769 (536 Female, 230 Male, 3 Unreported; Age M

= 39.18 , SD = 21.70; Race and Ethnicity: 19 Hispanic (2.5%), 591 White (76.9%), 37 Asian

(4.8%), 19 Black(2.5%), 30 More than one race (3.9%), 4 Other(0.5%),  69 Unreported(8.9%))

completed survey 2. All participants provided consent and ethics approval was obtained from the

Institutional Review Boards of affiliated institutions including New York University and New

School for Social Research (for details, see Hirst et al., 2009; 2015).

Questionnaires

For all surveys, participants reported the current intensity of their feelings concerning the

9/11 attack by responding to the prompt At this moment, how strongly or intensely do you feel

[sad/angry/fear/confusion/frustration/shock] about the attack? on a scale from 1(low) to 5

(high). In addition, for surveys 2, 3, and 4, participants reported the remembered intensity of

their feelings concerning 9/11 in the two weeks after the attack by responding to the prompt:

How strongly or intensely did you feel [sad/angry/fear/confusion/frustration/shock] about the

attack? For a detailed description of the survey, see Hirst et al. (2009, 2015).

Covid-19 Study


<!-- Page 14 -->


OVERESTIMATING NEGATIVE FEELINGS INTENSITY IN MEMORY

13

Participants

Participants were recruited from Prolific and Amazon Mechanical Turk online

crowdsourcing platforms at two periods during the Covid-19 pandemic. Informed consent was

obtained prior to beginning the experiment. At the first time point (T1; May 3, 2020 - Nov 16,

2020), 1810 participants (851 Female, 927 Male, 15 Other, 17 Unreported; Age M = 32.02, SD =

10.80) completed scales measuring state distress and a battery of questionnaires probing

subjective stress due to Covid-related stressors. Participants were later invited to participate in a

follow up at a second time point (T2; Aug 13, 2021 - Oct 7, 2021; interval M = 402, SD = 49

days; Supplementary Figure 1) in which they again completed all scales and questionnaires

administered at T1 as well as additional questions retrospectively probing memory for Covid-

related stress experienced at T1. A total of 726 participants (40.1%; 345 Female, 367 Male, 5

Other, 9 Unreported; Age M = 34.77, SD = 12.1; Race: 544 White (75%), 74 Asian (10%), 51

Black(7%), 45 More than one race (6.3%), 12 Other (1.7%); Ethnicity: 66 Hispanic (9%))

returned. This study was approved by the Harvard University Committee on the Use of Human

Subjects (IRB19-0789).

Covid-related Questionnaires and Psychological Scales

To assess subjective stress associated with Covid-19, we compiled a list of 17 Covid-

related stressors and asked participants to rate How much stress are you currently experiencing?

on a Likert scale from 1 (no stress at all) to 5 (a lot of stress). Probed stressors included

decreased socialization, increased obstacles to engaging in regular daily activities, and problems

obtaining basic needs such as paychecks and groceries (see Supplementary Table 10 for full list).

Participants could select N/A if they were not currently experiencing particular stressors. These

questions were completed at both time points.


<!-- Page 15 -->


OVERESTIMATING NEGATIVE FEELINGS INTENSITY IN MEMORY

14

At T2, after reporting current Covid-related stress, participants were reminded of when

they completed Survey 1 (when you first entered the study on MM/DD/YY…). They were next

instructed to recall their previously reported stress (Please try to remember how you might have

felt and responded then). Cueing presumably reduced the likelihood that participants would

report their average Covid-related previous stress, rather than their stress at T1. They were

subsequently presented with the list of stressors evaluated at T1 and rated their remembered

stress using the same scale as before. Again, they could select N/A if particular stressors were

considered irrelevant.

In addition to Covid-related stress, participants reported their emotional well-being by

completing the 10-item Perceived Stress Scale (PSS; Cohen et al., 1983) and 21-item short-form

Depression Anxiety Stress Scale (DASS-21; Henry & Crawford, 2005). These scales were

administered at both time points.

Statistical Analysis

Bayesian General Linear Models

Data were analyzed using R, version 4.0.2 (R Core Team, 2020). For our analyses, we

leveraged Bayesian Generalized Linear Models (BGLM). Utilizing BGLM allowed us to take

advantage of several Bayesian methods for evaluating the robustness of our results including

posterior predictive checks for model fit, and Highest Density Intervals (HDI) for evaluating the

uncertainty associated with parameter estimates. BGLM were implemented in R and interfaced

with Stan via the stan_glmer function in the rstanarm R package (version 2.21.1; Stan

Development Team, 2020). See Supplementary Methods for more detailed information regarding

Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) simulations.

Transparency and openness

We report how we determined our sample sizes, describe all date exclusion criteria, all

https://github.com/DaPsyientist/COVID911_EmoMem and data is available at

https://osf.io/kqe54/?view_only=beb4fcfe04b245969b03b761f721f44f. This study’s design and

analysis were not pre-registered.

## Results

To accommodate the data generating process of participants’ ratings (1-5), dependent

variables were transformed to lie between 0-1 for analysis with BGLMs using beta family

distributions (Smithson & Verkuilen, 2006; Branscum et al., 2007). Wherever participants had

differing numbers of ratings due to ‘N/A’ responses, a weighted beta regression method was

utilized whereby weight corresponded to the number of responses provided by a participant.

Prior evidence from simulations indicates the posterior direction (pd) statistic we report

possesses a linear relationship with the frequentist p-value (Makowski et al., 2019). As such, pd

can be interpreted as an index of effect existence, rather than statistical significance, which is

approximately equivalent to 1 - p-value. Unless otherwise noted, parameter estimates are

presented with median values and the highest density interval (HDI) at 95% threshold. Similar to

the frequentist confidence interval, the HDI describes a probabilistically likely range of posterior

distribution values for an effect size given the observed data and explicit model assumptions.

Participants experienced decreased negative feelings at one year follow-up, but

overestimated the intensity of past negative emotional experiences

We leveraged the 9/11 and Covid-19 datasets to characterize the relationship between

previous, current, and remembered negative emotional experiences. First, we assessed how the


<!-- Page 17 -->


OVERESTIMATING NEGATIVE FEELINGS INTENSITY IN MEMORY

16

intensity of negative emotions associated with the 9/11 attack changes from T1 to T2. To enable

comparisons between the Covid-19 and 9/11 datasets, we focused on ratings collected 2 weeks

and 1 year following the attack, respectively. We characterized overall intensity of negative

feelings by averaging participants’ ratings over six negative emotions (sadness, fear, anger,

confusion, frustration and shock), and utilized a mixed-effects BGLM with time point (T1/T2) as

a within-participant categorical predictor. Results from this analysis indicate the effect of time

has a 100% probability [pd] of being positive providing evidence that the intensity of negative

feelings experienced at T2 (2.81 ± 0.98) was lower than feelings at T1 (3.45 ± 0.82; M = -0.77,

HDI95% [-0.83, -0.70]; Figure 1a, Supplementary Table 1). In other words, people experienced less

intense negative feelings one year after the attack.

After establishing that the level of negative feelings decreased, we evaluated the

consistency of memory for feelings for the 9/11 attack. Following past work on memory for the

intensity of feelings (Levine et al., 2001; Levine et al., 2021), we compared the remembered

feelings reported at T2 with the overall intensity they reported at T1. Similar to our previous

analysis, we used a mixed-effects BGLM with memory type (T1/Remembered) as a within-

participant categorical predictor. Our results indicate the effect of remembering has a 100%

probability [pd] of being positive providing evidence that people recalled experiencing more

intense negative emotion (3.76 ± 0.75) than what they actually experienced (M = 0.40, HDI95%

[0.33, 0.46]; Figure 1a). In other words, people’s memory of feelings associated with the 9/11

attack was inconsistent, manifesting as overestimation in the intensity of their previous negative

emotional experience.

Following a similar analysis procedure, we examined how stress related to the Covid-19

pandemic changed over time. Overall stress was characterized by averaging stress ratings across


<!-- Page 18 -->


OVERESTIMATING NEGATIVE FEELINGS INTENSITY IN MEMORY

17

all 17 Covid-related stressors. The results were qualitatively similar to our 9/11 dataset: The

effect of time had a 100% probability [pd] of being negative providing evidence that stress

experienced at T2 (2.11 ± 0.81) was lower than stress at T1 (2.30 ± 0.84; M = -0.28, HDI95% [-

0.36, -0.21]; Figure 1b, Supplementary Table 2). In contrast, the effect of remembering has a

100% probability [pd] of being positive providing evidence that compared to actual stress at T1

(2.30 ± 0.84), remembered T1 stress was greater (2.40 ± 0.87; M = 0.20, HDI95%[0.13, 0.27];

*Figure 1b). Altogether, these results suggest that decreases in negative emotional experience and*

the inaccuracy of memory for these experiences is not unique to the 9/11 attack, but more

broadly applicable to negative emotional events such as the Covid-19 pandemic.

Compared to Covid-related stress, memory for the intensity of negative feelings associated

with the 9/11 attack was more inconsistent

After establishing a similar tendency to misremember negative emotional experiences

occurring one year prior, we examined whether the magnitude of emotional memory

inconsistency differs between the 9/11 and Covid-19 datasets. To this end, a memory deviation

index was calculated for each participant by subtracting remembered from previously

experienced feeling ratings. A positive memory deviation index indicates people recalled a

higher level of stress/negative feelings than what they previously experienced i.e., they

overestimated previous stress/negative feelings. Model regressors included a categorical variable

indicating the dataset (9-11/Covid-19) as well as previous ratings to control for baseline level

differences. We found the effect of 9/11 has a 100% probability [pd] of being positive providing

evidence that compared to Covid-related stress, memories for negative feelings elicited by 9/11

were more biased (M = 0.21, HDI95% [0.17, 0.26] , Supplementary Table 3), reflecting that

participants were more likely to overestimate the intensity of experienced negative feelings for

## Discussion

Our study aimed to examine four aspects regarding the intensity of remembered feelings

for the Covid-19 pandemic and the 9/11 attack: (1) how consistent or accurate the intensity of

remembered feelings were, (2) how current feelings influence memories for remembered

feelings, and (3) the association between remembered feelings and current well-being.

Assessing the consistency of remembered feelings for emotional experiences associated

with 9/11 demonstrated that the intensity of past feelings was inconsistently recalled.

Remembered feelings were also inaccurately recalled for our Covid-19 sample. Both samples


<!-- Page 26 -->


OVERESTIMATING NEGATIVE FEELINGS INTENSITY IN MEMORY

25

were associated with a tendency to overestimate the intensity of past negative emotional

experiences. On the surface this seems to conflict with past studies in which participants

remember the intensity of their past feelings accurately. However, these studies concluded

remembered feelings were accurately recalled based on the overall mean of accuracy across

participants. When the accuracy of each individual’s remembered feelings is considered, the

results reveal much variability with regard to how accurately the intensity of remembered

feelings are recalled. For instance, Levine and colleagues (2021) found that when participants

felt more negative over time about the 2016 US presidential election, they overestimated how

angry and scared they initially were, and underestimated happiness. Similarly, Schmidt and

colleagues (2021) found that individuals who currently felt worse and saw Brexit as more

consequential for the U.K. recalled stronger negative emotions than what they first reported. This

indicates that the accuracy of the intensity of remembered feelings depends on the valence of the

remembered feeling and individuals’ current appraisals. Our results differ from these past

election outcome studies in that we only examined events that are likely to elicit negative

emotions and the bias for remembered feelings across both our samples was larger and

directionally consistent. Our 9/11 sample also enabled us to generalize how the consistency of

remembered feelings changes over a longer time scale than one year. For the 9/11 attacks,

remembered feelings were most overestimated after three years – rising after the first year, and

returning to first year levels after ten years (Figure 3). This suggests the consistency of

remembered feelings varies non-linearly over time, but future research is necessary to determine

the generality of this non-linear relationship for other consequential events such as the Covid-19

pandemic.


<!-- Page 27 -->


OVERESTIMATING NEGATIVE FEELINGS INTENSITY IN MEMORY

26

In addition to characterizing the consistency of memory, we evaluated whether

remembered feelings were susceptible to similar biases as those observed in previous studies. In

their prior investigation of the intensity of remembered grief in widows, Safer and colleagues

(2001) uncovered a recency bias whereby the intensity of current grief was more predictive of

remembered grief than people’s initial grief. Schmidt and colleagues (2021) replicated and

expanded these findings by demonstrating that remembered negative emotions were biased by

current negative feelings in addition to appraisals regarding the consequentiality of the event. In

order to determine whether remembered feelings were biased by current emotional experience,

we investigated the influence of past and current emotional experience or stress on the

remembered intensity of negative events across our two samples. For accurate recollection,

current emotional experience should only be associated with remembered feelings insofar as

current and past feelings are similar. However, results from our two samples demonstrate that

both current and initial emotional experiences were involved in constructions of remembered

feelings. Furthermore, current experience predicted remembered feelings despite participants

currently experiencing lower levels of negative emotional experience or stress than either their

initial, or remembered, ratings. These results are consistent with those obtained in past studies on

the vulnerability of remembered emotion (Levine 1997; Safer et al., 2001) and highlight the

pervasive influence of current experience on remembered feelings.

Across both the 9/11 and the Covid-19 dataset, the intensity of remembered feelings was

overestimated with current emotional experience biasing remembered feelings. Beyond these

similarities, there was variation in our samples with regard to the magnitude of each effect.

Compared to Covid-related stress, the remembered intensity of negative feelings elicited by 9/11

was overestimated more. Furthermore, whereas the intensity of current and past emotional


<!-- Page 28 -->


OVERESTIMATING NEGATIVE FEELINGS INTENSITY IN MEMORY

27

experience was weighted equally in memories for the intensity of feelings experienced during

9/11, current stress had a larger influence than past stress on remembered feelings in our Covid-

19 sample – implicating a recency bias in recollection. There are several potential factors leading

to the observed differences in remembered negative feelings across our two datasets. One factor

is the temporal duration of these two events. Punctate, as opposed to prolonged, negatively

valenced events like 9/11 are temporally acute which likely facilitates recollections of feelings

that may not align with initial experience. In contrast, prolonged emotionally intense negative

events like Covid-19 may increase the difficulty of distinguishing recent experiences from those

at earlier time points resulting in an overreliance on recent experience when constructing a

memory.

In addition to the temporal duration of an autobiographical event, another potential factor

influencing remembered negative feelings is the way that the memory is probed. Specifically, the

Covid-19 survey at T2 asked participants how they felt when they first filled out the survey at

T1; in contrast, our 9/11 sample was tasked with recalling the intensity of their initial emotional

experience during the attack. Memory for feelings associated with the arbitrary date when

participants entered the study may be less rich than memories for a salient event like the 9/11

attack. Therefore, people rely more on their recent experience when reconstructing their

memories for dates that are arbitrarily imposed by the experimenter. This account is supported

by Safer et al. (2001), where the participants demonstrated a recency bias in their memory of

grief 6 months after the death of a spouse was probed i.e., during the extended period of grief.

Finally, the feelings probed in the two datasets also differ. The Covid-19 survey asked

participants to report their perceived stress related to 17 different stressors while the 9/11 survey

asked participants to rate 6 negative emotions. Although we conceptualized both studies as


<!-- Page 29 -->


OVERESTIMATING NEGATIVE FEELINGS INTENSITY IN MEMORY

28

examining negative feelings in the current paper, it is possible that the recall processes associated

with stress and negative emotions may be distinct. However, future experiments are necessary to

confirm the hypotheses above.

The final aspect we investigated about the intensity of remembered feelings was whether

there was an association between misremembered feelings and current well-being as measured

using the DASS and PSS. As well-being was not measured in the 9/11 sample, we only

examined this for our Covid-19 sample. Consistent with the finding that stress ratings decreased

over time, people’s well-being improved after one year. Critically, improvements in well-being

were negatively associated with overestimating past Covid-related stress: individuals who

improved the least in well-being tended to overestimate the intensity of their past negative

experience the most. This is consistent with previous work showing that widows whose grief

improved the most – signaling effective coping – tended to overestimate the intensity of past

negative experiences the least, a form of retrospective reappraisal (Safer et al., 2001). This

congruence suggests retrospective appraisal is occurring in our Covid-19 sample, with

improvements in well-being reflecting better coping with stress – although it is possible that

other factors may also be contributing to improved well-being, such as a general alleviation of

stress with time. We can not rule out these possibilities, but they are not mutually exclusive with

our arguments and notably the association between changes in well-being and memory bias

remains robust even after including current stress as a covariate in our model (Supplementary

*Table 8).*

These findings indicate both our samples were biased towards overestimating the

intensity of past negative feelings. Furthermore, our regression analysis suggests that

overestimating past negative feelings may be associated with decreased current well-being. This


<!-- Page 30 -->


OVERESTIMATING NEGATIVE FEELINGS INTENSITY IN MEMORY

29

pattern of results is consistent with research examining the relation between remembered grief

and well-being (Safer et al., 2001), but inconsistent with other research investigating how the

recollection of pre-exam anxiety relates to confidence in coping abilities (Keuler & Safer, 1998).

These discrepancies indicate that misremembering the intensity of negative feelings is generally

associated with changes to current well-being, but its effect may depend on situational context

and the nature of the emotional experiences.

In our current study we utilized the same 9/11 sample as Hirst et al. (2009) who

examined the consistency of remembered feelings by comparing how categorical negative

emotion labels used to describe an initial 9/11 experience changed over time. However, we used

an alternative measure of consistency which allows us to compare how memory for

consequential, emotional events varies as a result of how remembered feelings are defined. In

contrast to Hirst and colleagues, we evaluated how numerical ratings for the remembered

negative intensity of the initial 9/11 experience changed over time – a continuous measure of

consistency more commonly utilized in research examining the consistency of remembered

feelings (Levine et al., 2001; Kaplan et al., 2016; Safer et al., 2001; Schmidt et al., 2021; Levine

et al., 2021). These past studies generally demonstrate low rates of inaccuracy below 3%, but this

is likely the result of individual variability in memory biases depending on the valence of the

emotional event and individuals appraisals of its consequentiality. Compared to these past

studies, remembered feelings in our 9/11 sample were more inaccurate with a 9% rate of

overestimation. However, this is strikingly less than the 58% rate of inaccuracy obtained by Hirst

and colleagues when using a categorical measure of consistency with the same sample (Hirst et

al., 2009). This suggests that providing emotion labels as cues for subjects to use when

retrospectively rating their emotional experience likely minimizes variability because without


<!-- Page 31 -->


OVERESTIMATING NEGATIVE FEELINGS INTENSITY IN MEMORY

30

these labels, participants' categorical ratings would additionally require knowledge of the initial

rating scale. Indeed, Hirst and colleagues anticipated this confound and explicitly stated they

were not interested in participant’s memory for a particular score as this would require them to

remember the scale they used as well as their emotional intensity.

Our findings compliment past research on the consistency or accuracy of remembered

feelings for emotional experiences in three important ways. First, our results clarify that in

contrast to previous conclusions, remembered feelings for negatively valenced experiences are

inconsistent. Although past research suggests remembered feelings for emotional events are

accurately remembered, these results were likely confounded due to examining multiple

emotions with differing valences and memory biases from individuals varying appraisals of the

event. In contrast, memory in our 9/11 and Covid-19 samples was biased in a consistent manner

leading to general overestimation of the intensity of remembered feelings. Secondly, directly

comparing how the intensity of past emotional experiences was remembered across our two

samples indicates that not all negative events are remembered the same and the nature of an

event, way remembered feelings are probed, and type of remembered feelings may also play a

role in determining the overall accuracy of memory. These findings begin to delineate how the

temporal duration of an emotional event may impact remembered feelings and highlight the

necessity for further research contrasting memories for punctate and prolonged emotional events.

Lastly, leveraging different measures of consistency within the same sample suggested that the

overall inaccuracy of remembered feelings depends on how consistency is defined. Compared to

responses consisting of a categorical emotional label, inaccuracy was decreased when

participants numerically rated the intensity of their remembered feelings for prescribed emotions

– suggesting that measures probing the consistency of specified emotions may underestimate the


<!-- Page 32 -->


OVERESTIMATING NEGATIVE FEELINGS INTENSITY IN MEMORY

31

inaccuracy of remembered feelings. As a result, future studies should exercise caution when

deciding how to characterize the consistency of remembered feelings. Whereas evaluating the

consistency of intensity ratings for emotions enables the characterization of how specific

emotional experiences change over time, using categorical measures may provide a more

complete picture of the overall consistency of remembered feelings.

Constraints on generality

This study has a few limitations. First, we tried to shed light on people’s memory of negative

autobiographical events using datasets related to the 9/11 attack and Covid-19 pandemic, but our

findings may not generalize to events that are more personal and/or common in daily life, such as

quarreling with a friend. Although we laid out a handful of contextual factors related to the event

that could influence people’s remembered feelings, more research is needed to enable a

comprehensive understanding of the relationships between event features and the remembered

negative feelings. Second, selection bias may exist in our samples. For the 9/11 dataset, we

included people who completed at least one follow-up study instead of people who completed all

three questionnaires (1, 3, and 10 years after the attack). This data exclusion criterion was

established to obtain a relatively well-powered sample size, but risks ignoring people who

intentionally chose not to participate in future follow-ups. Similarly, for the Covid-19 sample,

some participants did not return to complete the follow-up study. Furthermore, both samples

were geographically located in the US which may limit how well our results generalize to

populations outside of the US. Finally, our study suggests that the consistency of memory is

sensitive to the manner in which recollection is probed - thus, the findings presented in this paper

may not generalize beyond the remembered intensity of negative emotional experiences.
